chunk_findings.detail: The change's stated intent enumerates the query kinds as `task|phase|bug|decision|lesson|research|session|memory|rule|item`, but `KINDS` registers only nine of them — `rule` is absent (and `_columns` likewise has no `"rule"` entry). Because `parse()` hard-rejects any kind not in `KINDS`, a document type that spells the documented query `query:kind=rule state=...` fails at load with `QueryError: query kind 'rule' is not one of task, phase, item, bug, decision, lesson, research, session, memory`, even though `rule` is a first-class record/concept elsewhere (a `ddflow/templates/doctypes/rules.toml` ships in this same change and the guidance itself references `ddflow rule list`). So the declared declarative-query surface is a strict subset of the spec: any operator or template using `kind=rule` gets a load-time rejection rather than matching rows, which is exactly the "declarative query without Python" capability the change is meant to provide.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/recordquery.py:72 (KINDS) / parse kind check

chunk_findings.detail: `run.err` is interpolated into the `SourceUnavailable` message without ever passing through `ctx.redactor`; only stdout is redacted (`text = ctx.redactor(run.out) if ctx.redactor else run.out`, line 42). The intent for this source states the output is "size-capped and redacted", and an unavailable section's reason is surfaced in the generated document (that is the whole point of "`unavailable` (never empty-and-passed)"). So for an operator-declared command whose stderr carries a secret — e.g. a tool that echoes a URL with an embedded token, or prints an auth error containing a credential — a failing run (`run.code != 0`) writes that raw secret into the section output, bypassing the redaction that was applied to the same command's stdout. The fix is to run `run.err` through the same redactor before putting it in the message (and similarly for `run.reason` on line 39 if it can carry process output).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/source_cmd.py:41

chunk_findings.detail: `read_capped` joins a caller-supplied `rel` onto `ctx.repo` and reads it with no resolution/containment check and no tracked-file check, even though its own docstring promises "The text of one tracked file" and the module promises file sources are "inside the repo". `check_relative` (the only path validator here) is lexical only: it rejects `..` components, backslashes and absolute paths, but it does not resolve symlinks and it does not reject drive-relative paths on Windows (`Path("C:secret.txt").is_absolute()` is `False`, so `check_relative` accepts it while `repo / "C:secret.txt"` produces a path on the C: drive), and, unlike `tracked_in`/`_template`, `read_capped` does not re-resolve. Concretely, with a repo root at `[REDACTED:path]`, `read_capped(ctx, "../outside.txt")` (or a path through a symlink planted inside the repo) happily `stat`s and `read_text`s `[REDACTED:path]` and returns its contents; nothing in this function raises `SourceError`, and the size cap is the only gate. It also silently falls back to the process CWD when `ctx.repo is None` (`(ctx.repo or Path())`), reading a file relative to wherever the process runs, whereas the sibling helper `tracked_in` correctly raises `SourceUnavailable` in that case. Any caller that relies on this helper for the safety its docstring advertises (i.e. validating the path with `check_relative` only, which is exactly the "path-safe, inside the repo" contract of the `file:` source) reads arbitrary files.

chunk_findings.detail: `search()` splits the query with `re.findall(r"\w+", query)` and bails out with an empty result for *every* mode when that list is empty. For the word-based paths that is correct, but `substring` mode is a literal trigram lookup, and the trigram tokenizer indexes every 3-character sequence of the text, punctuation included. Given a chunk whose text contains `...`, `-->`, `===`, `:::` or similar (extremely common in code/doc text), `idx.search("...", mode="substring")` returns `SearchResult(hits=(), mode="substring", note="")` before `_query` ever touches `chunks_tri`, so the user gets zero hits and no `note` explaining a degradation — even though the index holds the substring and the query satisfies the `MIN_SUBSTRING` check. The same silent empty result occurs for `-->`/`===`/`:::` etc. The guard must be restricted to the `words`/`like` paths (e.g. only return early when there are no words *and* the mode is not `substring`), otherwise the trigram index cannot answer exactly the literal-substring searches it was created for.

chunk_findings.detail: `assert plain.search("100%_").hits == ()  # LIKE wildcards are literal` cannot detect the behavior it names. The `repo` fixture contains only `README.md` ("start here"), `docs/guide.md` (widget/Usage text) and `docs/other.md` (gardens) — no chunk contains the substring `100`, let alone `100%_`. In LIKE mode the correct (escaped) query matches nothing, and an unescaped pattern `%100%_%` also matches nothing, because no indexed text contains `100` followed by any character. So the assertion passes whether or not the implementation escapes `%`/`_`. A regression that turns the query into an unescaped LIKE pattern (which would over-match any chunk containing `100<x>`) is not caught by this test. To actually exercise the literal-wildcard property the fixture needs a document whose content contains `100` plus a following character (e.g. `100%` or `100x`), so that an unescaped `%100%_%` would wrongly hit while the escaped literal query does not.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's stated intent enumerates the queryable kinds as `task|phase|bug|decision|lesson|research|session|memory|rule|item` (ten kinds), but the `KINDS` registry defines only nine: `task`, `phase`, `item`, `bug`, `decision`, `lesson`, `research`, `session`, `memory` — `rule` is absent, and the parallel `_columns` mapping used by `parse` for `sort`/`fields` validation is missing `rule` too. Given the input `query:kind=rule state=active` (a rule section, the exact use case the intent promises: "a declarative, safe record query over State — kind (... |rule|item)"), `parse` reaches `kind = words.get("kind", "")` and raises `QueryError("query kind 'rule' is not one of task, phase, item, bug, decision, lesson, research, session, memory")`, so any doctype section authored against the promised kind set fails to load instead of selecting the rules. Either the kind registry must gain a `"rule": RecordKind(...)`/`records.Rule` entry (with its `state`/`owner`/date columns), or the intent's kind list must drop `rule`; as written, the implementation contradicts the spec it is derived from.

chunk_findings.detail: This change raises a guard ratchet by two entries (+2 -0) in `tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml` at the same time as it adds new functions to the shipped tree (`ddflow/services/doctypes/source_kind.py` `_template`, `ddflow/services/doctypes/source_file.py` `section_of`, etc.). The baseline file exists to record functions that no production code calls; growing it means two additional newly-added functions are dead in the shipped code and were accepted into the ratchet instead of being wired up or removed. [D-cleanup-before-pause] records the operator decision to "take the ratchets down" before the pause, and explicitly frames cleanup as deleting the old/unused code rather than carrying new unreferenced surface. Editing the baseline upward moves the ratchet in the opposite direction; the smallest reproducer is to run the guard over this tree and observe that the only way it passes is via the newly added baseline lines, i.e. the check no longer constrains the two new functions at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The comment says "LIKE wildcards are literal", but this assertion cannot distinguish a correct implementation from one that fails to escape `%`/`_` into the fallback `LIKE` pattern. With the corpus built by the `repo` fixture (README.md "start here", docs/other.md "gardens", docs/guide.md "How to install the widget. Run the widget daily.") no chunk contains the substring `100`, so an escaped pattern `%100\%\_%` and an unescaped pattern `%100%_%` both return zero rows and the test stays green even if the escaping is missing.
